Sanatsujata provides teachings on the true qualities of a Brahmin and the path to the eternal world.

extraction_text: Dhritarashtra asks about the eternal world belonging to those who follow their own dharma and the different sequences among the twice-born caused by karma.
Sanatsujata describes the qualities and afterlife of true Brahmins, who are powerful like wrestlers, shine in heaven, and live without sorrow where food and drink are abundant.
Sanatsujata teaches that a true Brahmin remains silent in the face of threats, does not covet Brahmin property, and lives discreetly among relatives without revealing his actions.

Sanatsujata states that no Brahmin can kill the inner soul (Atman) because he sees Brahman dwelling there, and a true Brahmin is learned in the Vedas, not weary, not acquisitive, honored, and free from sorrow.

Sanatsujata distinguishes between mere ritual performers and truly honored individuals, teaching that one should remain equanimous whether honored or not, understanding that honor comes from the wise and lack of honor from the ignorant.

Sanatsujata explains that honor/pride and austerity/silence do not go together, with honor belonging to this world and austerity to the other world, and that auspiciousness (shri) has six gates to guard against pride and delusion: truth, uprightness, modesty, self-control, purity, and knowledge.
The text concludes by identifying itself as Chapter 42 of the Udyoga Parva (The Book of Effort) in the Mahabharata.
